stories.headline: Sea turtles nest on California beaches for the first time
stories.summary: Two olive ridley turtles laid eggs at Seal Beach and Huntington Beach, a first for the US West Coast. Before storms hit, wildlife teams moved 204 eggs to incubators at the Aquarium of the Pacific.
stories.why: These turtles usually nest in Mexico and Central America. Their hatchlings could be California's first.

stories.headline: A 'Cretaceous rabbit' fossil solves a 40-year mystery
stories.summary: Tamirkhan, a 6–7 inch mammal that lived alongside dinosaurs, is the most complete zhelestid ever found. Described in Nature, it shows this group wasn't related to today's placental mammals after all.
stories.why: For decades scientists judged these animals by their teeth alone. A full skeleton changed the story.

stories.headline: A snake missing since 1872 turns up on a road in India
stories.summary: A forest patrol near Bhuj photographed an Afro-Asian sand snake, the first confirmed record in Kutch in over 150 years. The last specimens were collected by naturalist Ferdinand Stoliczka in 1871–72.
stories.why: It links a 19th-century record to today, proof that dry, overlooked landscapes still hide wildlife.

stories.headline: Two Brazilian birds scream louder than 120 decibels
stories.summary: Biologists found that the bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema both break 120 decibels, joining the white bellbird, clocked at 125 dB in 2019. That's louder than a jackhammer.
stories.why: Around 120 dB seems to be the physical limit for birds, so Brazil may hold the world's loudest.

fun_fact: Red-legged seriemas sing in duets, pairs trading calls back and forth like a squabbling couple.
